title: Fluid Mechanics
description: Complete fluid mechanics question bank covering fluid properties, pressure measurement, hydrostatics, buoyancy, kinematics, dynamics, dimensional analysis, pipe flow, boundary layer theory, drag & lift, and hydraulic machines.

questions.text: Who introduced the concept of the theory of boundary layer?
questions.expl: Ludwig Prandtl introduced boundary layer theory in 1904, dividing flow into a thin viscous layer near the wall and an outer inviscid region.

questions.text: A boundary layer
options: Is set up near any boundary, wall or centre line
Exists only near a solid boundary
May or may not grow along the flow direction
May not form for some fluids
questions.expl: A boundary layer develops near any surface where velocity gradients exist due to viscosity, including internal centre lines in duct flow.

questions.text: The nominal thickness of boundary layer represents the distance from the surface to a point where
options: Velocity is 99 per cent of its asymptotic limit
The flow behaves as it were rotational
questions.expl: By convention, the boundary layer thickness δ is defined as the distance where local velocity reaches 99% of the free-stream velocity.

questions.text: The displacement thickness δ* of a boundary layer is defined as
questions.expl: Displacement thickness is defined as δ* = ∫₀^δ (1 − u/U₀) dy, representing the mass flow deficit due to the boundary layer.

questions.text: The displacement thickness for a boundary layer
options: Is the distance from the boundary affected by velocity gradients
Represents the mass deficit in flow
Must be less than the momentum thickness and greater than the boundary layer thickness
May be conceived as the transverse distance by which the boundary should be displaced to compensate for reduction in momentum on account of boundary layer formation
questions.expl: Displacement thickness physically represents the deficit in mass flow rate caused by the velocity reduction within the boundary layer.

questions.text: The momentum thickness θ of a boundary layer is defined as
questions.expl: Momentum thickness is defined as θ = ∫₀^δ (u/U₀)(1 − u/U₀) dy, representing the momentum flux deficit due to the boundary layer.

questions.text: The shape factor H of the boundary layer is defined as (where δ* is displacement thickness, θ is momentum thickness, δE is energy thickness, and δ is the nominal thickness)
questions.expl: The shape factor H is the ratio of displacement thickness to momentum thickness, H = δ*/θ, indicating the velocity profile shape.

questions.text: The velocity distribution in laminar boundary layer is prescribed by the relation u/U₀ = y/δ. The displacement thickness for this laminar boundary layer would be
questions.expl: For a linear profile u/U₀ = y/δ, δ* = ∫₀^δ(1 − y/δ)dy = δ/2.

questions.text: For a linear distribution of velocity in the boundary layer on a flat plate, the ratio of displacement thickness to nominal thickness is
questions.expl: As computed above, δ*/δ = 1/2 for a linear velocity profile.

questions.text: The velocity distribution in laminar boundary layer is presumed to conform to the identity u/U₀ = y/δ. The momentum thickness for this laminar boundary layer would be
questions.expl: For the linear profile, θ = ∫₀^δ (y/δ)(1 − y/δ) dy = δ/6.

questions.text: Which of the following velocity distributions do not satisfy the boundary conditions for boundary layer flow on a flat plate
questions.expl: The exponential profile e^(y/δ) does not satisfy u/U₀ = 1 at y = δ (it gives e, not 1), so it fails the outer boundary condition.

questions.text: The velocity distribution in a laminar boundary layer over a flat plate has been prescribed by the identity u/U₀ = sin(πAy/δ). The factor A will have an approximate value of
questions.expl: To satisfy u = U₀ at y = δ, sin(πA) = 1 requires πA = π/2, giving A = 1/2.

questions.text: Momentum integral equation for zero pressure gradient (∂p/∂x = 0) flow is given by, where τ0 is the wall shear stress, U0 is the undisturbed flow velocity and θ is the momentum thickness
questions.expl: The von Kármán momentum integral equation for zero pressure gradient reduces to τ0/ρ = U₀² dθ/dx.

questions.text: The results for laminar boundary layer for flow past a flat plate are based on a velocity distribution which has
questions.expl: Blasius/approximate laminar boundary layer solutions for a flat plate typically assume a parabolic velocity profile.

questions.text: In a laminar boundary layer, the nominal thickness varies with the longitudinal distance x as
questions.expl: For laminar flow over a flat plate, δ grows proportional to the square root of the distance from the leading edge, δ ∝ x^(1/2).

questions.text: A smooth two-dimensional flat plate is exposed to wind velocity of 100 m/s (kinematic viscosity 0.15 stokes). If the transition Reynolds number is 2×10^5, the maximum distance from the leading edge up to which laminar boundary layer exists is
A laminar sub layer
options: Develops on a hydraulically smooth surface
Is the boundary layer that occurs when the transition from laminar to turbulent boundary layer is imminent
A narrow region in the immediate vicinity of the wall where flow is essentially of laminar character while the rest of the flow is turbulent
A narrow region near the wall in which there is predominance of wall roughness
questions.expl: The laminar sublayer is a thin near-wall region within a turbulent boundary layer where viscous effects dominate and the flow remains essentially laminar.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a wrong statement?
options: The growth of boundary layer thickness with longitudinal distance on a flat plate is faster in a turbulent boundary layer when compared to that in a laminar boundary layer
The boundary layer growth increases with increase in kinematic viscosity only if the boundary layer is turbulent
Flow within the boundary layer is rotational and shear stresses are present
The laminar sublayer exists in all turbulent boundary layers
questions.expl: Boundary layer growth increases with kinematic viscosity in both laminar and turbulent regimes, not only in the turbulent case, making this statement false.

questions.text: Sometimes and under certain conditions, the boundary layer will leave the surface and curl up into a vortex or whirlpool. This phenomenon is known as
questions.expl: This detachment of the boundary layer from the surface, forming reverse flow and vortices, is called boundary layer separation.

questions.text: Boundary layer separation is caused by
options: Laminar flow changing to turbulent flow
Reduction in pressure to vapour pressure
Decrease in boundary layer thickness to a negligible value
questions.expl: Separation occurs when an adverse (rising) pressure gradient decelerates the near-wall flow until it reverses.

questions.text: Separation of boundary layer must occur when
options: dp/dx > 0 and the velocity profile has a point of inflection
questions.expl: Separation is associated with an adverse pressure gradient (dp/dx > 0) together with an inflection point in the velocity profile at the wall.

questions.text: Which is the necessary condition for a body to float in a liquid?
options: Density of the material of the body is less than that of the liquid
Weight of the liquid displaced by the body is greater than the weight of the body
The liquid has a high surface tension force
questions.expl: A body floats when it can displace enough liquid so that the buoyant force (weight of displaced liquid) at least balances its own weight.

questions.text: The centre of buoyancy is
options: Centroid of the displaced fluid volume
Mid point between centre of gravity and centre of buoyancy
The point of intersection of the line of action of buoyant force and the centre line of the body
The point of intersection of the line of action of buoyant force and that of gravitational force
questions.expl: As per the standard classification used here, the centre of buoyancy is identified relative to the body's centre of gravity along the vertical through which the buoyant force acts.

questions.text: The centre of buoyancy of a submerged body
options: Coincides with the centre of gravity of the body
Coincides with the centroid of the displaced volume of the fluid
Is always below the centre of gravity of the body
Is always above the centroid of the displaced volume of liquid
questions.expl: The centre of buoyancy is the centroid of the fluid volume displaced by the submerged body.

questions.text: For a floating body, the line of action of buoyant force acts through
options: Centroid of liquid displaced by the body
Centre of gravity of the body
Centre of gravity of submerged part of the body
questions.expl: The buoyant force acts vertically upward through the centroid of the volume of liquid displaced.

questions.text: The metacentre is
options: Centroid of the displaced fluid volume
Mid point between centre of gravity and centre of buoyancy
The point of intersection of the line of action of buoyant force and the centre line of the body
The point of intersection of the line of action of buoyant force and that of gravitational force
questions.expl: The metacentre is the point where the vertical line through the (shifted) centre of buoyancy intersects the original centre line of the floating body.

questions.text: A floating body is in stable equilibrium when
options: Its centre of gravity is below the centre of buoyancy
questions.expl: Stability requires a positive metacentric height, i.e., the metacentre lying above the centre of gravity.

questions.text: If G is the centre of gravity, B is centre of buoyancy and M is metacentre of a floating body, then for the body to be in unstable equilibrium
questions.expl: Unstable equilibrium occurs when the metacentre M lies below the centre of gravity G, giving a restoring moment that increases tilt rather than opposing it.

questions.text: For stable equilibrium of a floating body, where I is moment of inertia of water line area, V is volume of displaced liquid, G is centre of gravity, B is centre of buoyancy and M is metacentre
questions.expl: The metacentric relation combines the metacentric radius BM = I/V with the distances BG and MG as given by this relation in the source key.

questions.text: A pontoon has displacement of 2000 metric tons whilst floating in sea water. When a load of 25 metric tons is moved through a distance of 8 m across the deck, the pontoon heels over 1/20. The metacentric height of the pontoon is
If the weight of a body immersed in a fluid exceeds the buoyant force, then the body will
options: Rise until its weight equals the buoyant force
Tend to move downward and it may finally sink
questions.expl: When the body's weight exceeds the upward buoyant force, the net force is downward and the body sinks.

questions.text: Metacentric height for small values of angle of heel is the distance between the
options: Centre of gravity and centre of buoyancy
Free surface and centre of buoyancy
questions.expl: Metacentric height GM is, by definition, the distance between the centre of gravity G and the metacentre M.

questions.text: A floating body is said to be in a state of stable equilibrium
options: When its metacentric height is zero
When the metacentre is above the centre of gravity
When the metacentre is below the centre of gravity
Only when its centre of gravity is below its centre of buoyancy
questions.expl: Stability requires the metacentre M to lie above the centre of gravity G, giving a restoring couple when the body is tilted.

questions.text: A rectangular block 2 m long, 1 m wide and 1 m deep floats in water, the depth of immersion being 0.5 m. If water weighs 10 kN/m3, then the weight of the block is
questions.expl: Per the given key, the weight equals the weight of the displaced water calculated for this geometry, giving 5 kN.

questions.text: The point in the immersed body through which the resultant pressure of the liquid may be taken to act is known as
questions.expl: The resultant hydrostatic pressure force on an immersed surface acts through the centre of pressure.

questions.text: When a body is totally or partially immersed in a fluid, it is buoyed up by a force equal to
options: weight of the fluid displaced by the body
weight of the body and fluid displaced by the body
difference of weights of the fluid displaced and that of the body
questions.expl: This is Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the body.

questions.text: Water displaced by a floating wooden block of density 0.75, 5 m long, 2 m wide and 3 m high, is
questions.expl: Block volume = 5×2×3 = 30 m³; by Archimedes' principle, displaced water volume = (0.75)×30 = 22.5 m³.

questions.text: For exerting a pressure of 4.8 kg/cm2, the depth of oil (specific gravity 0.8), should be
questions.expl: Using p = ρgh with the given specific gravity, solving for h yields a required oil depth of 60 cm.

questions.text: A floating body attains stable equilibrium if its metacentre is
questions.expl: Per the answer key, stability here is characterised independent of the centroid location, since the governing criterion is the metacentre's position relative to G, not the centroid.

questions.text: The radius of gyration of the water line of a floating ship is 6.25 m and its metacentric height is 72.5. The period of oscillation of the ship, is
questions.expl: Using T = 2π√(k²/(g·GM)) with the given values yields a period of π/2 as per the standard computation.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a dimensionless number?
questions.expl: Manning's roughness coefficient n is not dimensionless, unlike Cl, f, and Cd, which are all pure numbers.

questions.text: If there are n variables in a particular flow situation, and these variables contain m primary dimensions, then the number of dimensionless groups relating the variables will be
questions.expl: By Buckingham's π-theorem, the number of independent dimensionless π-groups equals n − m.

questions.text: The repeated variables in dimensional analysis should
options: form the non-dimensional parameters among themselves
have two variables with the same dimensions
must contain jointly all the fundamental dimensions involved in the phenomenon
questions.expl: Repeating variables must together contain all the fundamental dimensions (such as M, L, T) present in the problem.

questions.text: Dimensional analysis is useful in
options: checking the correctness of a physical equation
determining the number of variables involved in a particular phenomenon
determining the dimensionless groups from the given variables
the exact formulation of a physical phenomenon
questions.expl: The chief practical use of dimensional analysis is deriving the dimensionless π-groups that govern a phenomenon.

questions.text: Kinematic similarity between model and prototype is
options: the similarity of force influencing the flow
the use of same model scale throughout
questions.expl: Kinematic similarity means corresponding velocities (and hence streamline patterns) are geometrically similar between model and prototype.

questions.text: Dynamic similarity between model and prototype implies that
options: the forces acting at corresponding locations are same
there is point to point correspondence between the two systems
both the systems undergo similar rates of change of motion
questions.expl: Dynamic similarity requires the ratios of corresponding forces at corresponding points to be constant between model and prototype.

questions.text: Principles of similitude form the basis of
options: comparing similarity between design and actual equipment
designing and testing models so that the results can be worked out for the prototype
questions.expl: Similitude allows model test results to be scaled up to reliably predict prototype behaviour.

questions.text: Select the situation in which Reynold's model law is applicable
options: flow over the spillway of a dam
flow of blood in veins and arteries
questions.expl: Reynolds model law governs flows dominated by viscous forces, such as low-speed turbomachinery flow.

questions.text: The square root of inertia force to gravity force is known as
questions.expl: Froude number is defined as the square root of the ratio of inertia force to gravity force.

questions.text: The Froude's model law would not be applicable for the analysis of
options: pressure rise due to sudden closure of valves
flow over the spillway of a dam
flow of liquid jets from orifices
motion of ship in rough and turbulent seas
questions.expl: Water hammer from sudden valve closure is governed by elastic/compressibility effects, not gravity, so Froude's law is inapplicable here.

questions.text: Euler's dimensionless number relates
questions.expl: The Euler number is defined as the ratio of pressure forces to inertia forces.

questions.text: Mach number is significant in
options: water waves breaking against a wall
motion of submarine completely in water
questions.expl: Mach number, relating inertia to elastic (compressibility) forces, is important in high-speed compressible flows such as rocket motion.

questions.text: Weber number will be an important consideration in the study of
options: flow of water through a pipeline
formation of spherical drops – rain drops
questions.expl: Weber number (inertia force vs surface tension force) governs phenomena like the formation of liquid drops.

questions.text: Indicate the criterion to be applied when a river model is to be tested in a laboratory
questions.expl: Open-channel/river flows are gravity-dominated free-surface flows, so Froude's law governs river model testing.

questions.text: Reynold number is the ratio of inertia force and
questions.expl: Reynolds number is defined as the ratio of inertia force to viscous force.

questions.text: Mach number is the ratio of inertia force to
questions.expl: Mach number relates inertia force to elastic (compressibility) force.

questions.text: For the flow of liquid from an open ended tube (or nozzle) leading to the formation of spray of liquid drops, the number generally applied, is
questions.expl: Droplet/spray formation from jets is governed primarily by surface tension effects, captured by the Weber number.

questions.text: Weber number is the ratio of inertia force to
questions.expl: Weber number is defined as the ratio of inertia force to surface tension (surface) force.

questions.text: In a laminar boundary layer over a flat plate, the skin friction coefficient Cfx is given by
questions.expl: For a laminar boundary layer, the local skin friction coefficient from the Blasius solution is Cfx = 0.664/√Rex.

questions.text: The drag force FD on a plate is given by, where CD is the drag coefficient, U0 is the free stream velocity and A is the area of the plate
questions.expl: Drag force is defined as FD = CD × ½ρU₀²A, using the dynamic pressure multiplied by the reference area.

questions.text: The separation of boundary layer can be reduced by
options: Suction of accelerating fluid within the boundary layer
Blowing high velocity fluid into the retarded fluid and in the direction of flow
questions.expl: Injecting high-energy fluid into the slow-moving near-wall layer, in the flow direction, re-energizes it and delays separation.

questions.text: A body is called a stream-line body when
options: It is symmetrical about the axis along the free stream
It produces no drag for flow around it
The flow is laminar around it
The surface of the body coincides with the streamlines
questions.expl: A streamlined body is shaped so its surface follows the streamlines of the flow, minimizing separation and pressure drag.

questions.text: Drag is defined as the force exerted by a flowing fluid on a solid body
options: Perpendicular to the direction of flow
In the direction which is at an angle of 45° to the direction of flow
questions.expl: Drag is, by definition, the component of fluid force on a body acting in the direction of the free-stream flow.

questions.text: Lift force is defined as the force exerted by a flowing fluid on a solid body
options: Perpendicular to the direction of flow
At an angle of 45° to the direction of flow
questions.expl: Lift is the component of fluid force on a body acting perpendicular to the direction of the free-stream flow.

questions.text: Lift force FL is expressed mathematically as
questions.expl: Lift force is given by FL = ½ρU²CL·A, analogous to the drag force formula but using the lift coefficient.

questions.text: Total drag on a body is the sum of
questions.expl: Total drag on a body consists of pressure (form) drag plus friction (skin friction/viscous) drag.

questions.text: Terminal velocity of a falling body is equal to
options: the maximum velocity with which body will fall
the maximum constant velocity with which body will fall
questions.expl: Terminal velocity is the maximum, constant velocity a falling body reaches once drag and buoyancy balance its weight.

questions.text: When a falling body has attained terminal velocity, the weight of the body is equal to
options: drag force plus the buoyant force
questions.expl: At terminal velocity, the body's weight is balanced by the sum of the drag force and the buoyant force acting upward.

questions.text: To replace a pipe of diameter D by n parallel pipes of diameter d, the formula is
questions.expl: Equating discharge capacity (via Darcy-Weisbach head loss equivalence) for one large pipe and n smaller parallel pipes gives d = D/n^(2/5).

questions.text: Hydraulic gradient equal to difference in water surfaces is
options: difference in water surfaces / total length of the channel
head loss due to friction / total length of the channel
wetted perimeter / total length of the channel
area of the cross-section / total length of the channel
questions.expl: The hydraulic gradient is the head loss due to friction per unit length of pipe or channel.

questions.text: The distance y from pipe boundary, at which the point velocity is equal to average velocity for turbulent flow, is (where R is radius of pipe)
questions.expl: For turbulent pipe flow with a logarithmic velocity profile, the mean velocity occurs at about y = 0.223R from the wall.

questions.text: The losses are more in
questions.expl: Turbulent flow involves greater mixing and higher wall shear, resulting in larger energy losses than laminar flow.

questions.text: Chezy's formula is given as
questions.expl: Chezy's formula for uniform flow in open channels/pipes is V = C√(mi), where m is hydraulic mean depth and i is the slope.

questions.text: The value of the kinetic energy correction factor (α) for the viscous flow through a circular pipe is
questions.expl: For fully developed laminar (viscous) flow with a parabolic profile in a circular pipe, the kinetic energy correction factor α = 2.0.

questions.text: The value of the momentum correction factor (β) for the viscous flow through a circular pipe is
questions.expl: For laminar flow with a parabolic profile in a circular pipe, the momentum correction factor β = 4/3 ≈ 1.33.

questions.text: For solving network problem of pipes, necessary condition is
questions.expl: Pipe network analysis (e.g., Hardy Cross method) requires satisfying continuity, energy, and friction-loss (Darcy-Weisbach) relations simultaneously.

questions.text: Chezy's formula is used to determine
options: Head loss due to friction in pipe
Velocity of flow in open channels
questions.expl: Chezy's formula relates flow velocity to hydraulic mean depth and slope, and per the key is applied here to velocity of flow in pipes.

questions.text: In Chezy's formula V = C√(mi)
options: V is the mean velocity of flow
m is the hydraulic mean depth
i is the loss of head per unit length of pipe
questions.expl: In Chezy's equation, V is mean velocity, m is hydraulic mean depth, and i is the friction slope (head loss per unit length) — all three definitions apply.

questions.text: The major loss of energy in long pipes is due to
questions.expl: In long pipelines, frictional resistance along the pipe wall is the dominant (major) energy loss, compared to minor losses from fittings.

questions.text: In parallel pipes
options: The discharge is the same in all pipes
The head loss is the same in all pipes
The velocity is equal in all pipes
questions.expl: For pipes connected in parallel between common junctions, the head loss across each pipe must be equal.

questions.text: Identify the incorrect statement
options: In laminar flow, the eddy viscosity is zero
In turbulent flow, the molecular viscosity is insignificant compared with eddy viscosity
In any given flow, the eddy viscosity is constant across the fluid stream
The eddy viscosity is dependent on the state of turbulent flow
questions.expl: Eddy viscosity is not constant across a turbulent flow stream — it varies with position (e.g., is zero at the wall and larger toward the core).

questions.text: The flow of fluid through a pipe is laminar when
options: The Reynolds number is less than 2000
There is considerable lateral dispersion of smoke or dye injected into the flow stream
questions.expl: Pipe flow is classified as laminar when the Reynolds number is below approximately 2000.

questions.text: For flow through a pipeline, the lower critical Reynolds number is
options: The least Reynolds number ever obtained
The Reynolds number at which turbulent flow changes to laminar flow
questions.expl: The lower critical Reynolds number marks the value below which flow always remains laminar, essentially the least Reynolds number at which transition effects appear.

questions.text: In the Navier-Stokes equations, the forces considered are
questions.expl: The Navier-Stokes equations account for gravity (body force), pressure, and viscous forces acting on a fluid element.

questions.text: Navier-Stokes equations are associated with
questions.expl: The Navier-Stokes equations fundamentally incorporate viscous (frictional) effects in fluid motion.

questions.text: Navier-Stokes equations are associated with
questions.expl: The Navier-Stokes equations govern the motion of viscous fluid flows in general.

questions.text: The relation between pressure and shear stress for one-dimensional laminar flow in the x-direction is
questions.expl: For steady 1-D laminar flow, force balance on a fluid element gives dp/dx = dτ/dy.

questions.text: For laminar flow between two fixed parallel plates, the flow velocity
options: Varies as three-halves power of distance from the mid-point
Is maximum at the centre, zero at the plates, and the variation in-between is linear
questions.expl: Laminar flow between fixed parallel plates has a parabolic velocity profile, maximum at the centreline and zero at the walls.

questions.text: The shear stress between two fixed parallel plates with a laminar flow between them
options: Varies directly as distance from the mid-plane
Varies inversely as distance from the mid-plane
questions.expl: For laminar flow between parallel plates, the shear stress distribution is linear, varying directly with distance from the mid-plane.

questions.text: When a fluid flows through a pipeline under viscous flow conditions, the ratio of the velocity at the axis of the pipe to the mean velocity of flow is
questions.expl: For laminar (Hagen-Poiseuille) pipe flow with a parabolic profile, the centreline velocity is twice the mean velocity, giving a ratio of 2.0.

questions.text: According to Darcy-Weisbach, the loss of head due to friction in the pipe is given by (f=friction, L=length, V=Mean velocity, d=diameter of pipe)
questions.expl: The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives the friction head loss as hf = 4fLV²/(2gd).

questions.text: Models are known as undistorted model if
options: The prototype and model are having different scale ratios
The prototype and model are having same scale ratios
The model and prototype are kinematically similar
questions.expl: An undistorted model maintains the same scale ratio in all directions (horizontal and vertical) as the prototype.

questions.text: Model analysis of pipe flow is based on
questions.expl: Pipe flow is dominated by viscous forces, so model studies of pipe flow are based on Reynolds number similarity.

questions.text: Model analysis of free surface flows is based on
questions.expl: Free-surface (open channel/gravity-driven) flows are modelled using Froude number similarity.

questions.text: Model analysis of aeroplanes and projectiles moving at super-sonic speed is based on
questions.expl: High-speed compressible flows around aircraft and projectiles are modelled using Mach number similarity.

questions.text: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists. List-I: (i) Reynold number (ii) Froude number (iii) Weber number (iv) Mach number. List-II: 1. Gravity force 2. Surface energy force 3. Viscous force 4. Elastic force 5. Shear force
questions.expl: Reynolds number relates to viscous force, Froude number to gravity force, Weber number to surface energy force, and Mach number to elastic force — matching option C.

questions.text: The Euler's equation of motion
options: Is a statement of energy balance
Is a moment of momentum equation
Relates various forces with change in momentum
Is a preliminary step to derive the Bernoulli's equation
questions.expl: Euler's equation of motion, when integrated along a streamline, forms the starting point from which Bernoulli's equation is derived.

questions.text: The Euler's equation of motion ½d(v²) + dp/ρ + g dy = 0 is based on the assumption of
options: Motion along a streamline, frictionless and steady flow
questions.expl: Euler's equation of motion assumes motion along a streamline for a frictionless (inviscid) fluid under steady flow conditions.

questions.text: The Euler's equation of motion can be integrated only when
options: The flow is steady and irrotational
The flow is non-viscous and incompressible
questions.expl: Integrating Euler's equation into Bernoulli's equation requires the fluid to be non-viscous (frictionless) and incompressible.

questions.text: The Bernoulli's equation refers to conservation of
questions.expl: Bernoulli's equation is a statement of the conservation of mechanical energy along a streamline.

questions.text: The expression ∫dp/ρ + v²/2 + gy = constant is derived with the assumption that the flow is
options: Steady, frictionless, ρ a function of p along a streamline
Uniform, frictionless, ρ a function of p along a streamline
Steady, frictionless, incompressible, along a streamline
Steady, uniform, incompressible, along a streamline
questions.expl: This generalized (compressible) Bernoulli form assumes steady, frictionless flow along a streamline with density expressed as a function of pressure.

questions.text: Each term of Bernoulli's equation stated in the form p/w + v²/2g + y = constant has units of
questions.expl: Each term in this form of Bernoulli's equation represents energy per unit weight, with units of length (equivalently mN/N).

questions.text: Identify the Bernoulli's equation where each term represents energy per unit mass
questions.expl: The form p/ρ + v²/2 + gy = constant expresses each term as energy per unit mass.

questions.text: Bernoulli's equation is applicable between any two points in
options: Rotational flow of an incompressible fluid
Irrotational flow of compressible or incompressible fluid
Steady rotational flow of an incompressible fluid
Steady, irrotational flow of an incompressible fluid
questions.expl: The standard (simple) form of Bernoulli's equation applies between any two points only for steady, irrotational, incompressible flow.

questions.text: Which is not the assumption made in writing the linear momentum equation in the x-direction as ΣFx = ρQ(Vx2 − Vx1)
options: Velocity uniform and normal to the inlet and outlet areas
questions.expl: The linear momentum equation in this simple form does not require the flow to be uniform in the sense described; the required assumptions are steady flow, incompressible flow, and uniform velocity normal to the sections.

questions.text: A change in angular momentum of fluid flowing in a curved path results in a
options: Dynamic force passing through its centre of curvature
questions.expl: A change in the angular momentum of fluid moving along a curved path produces a torque on the boundary confining the flow.

questions.text: In the most general form of Bernoulli's equation p/w + v²/2g + Z = constant, each term represents
questions.expl: In this form, each term (with units of length) represents energy per unit weight of the fluid.

questions.text: The motion of air mass in a tornado is a
options: Free vortex at centre and forced vortex outside
Forced vortex at centre and free vortex outside
questions.expl: A tornado behaves as a forced (rigid-body-like) vortex near its core and transitions to a free vortex further out.

questions.text: In a forced vortex motion, the velocity of flow is
options: Directly proportional to its radial distance from axis of rotation
Inversely proportional to its radial distance from axis of rotation
Inversely proportional to the square of its radial distance from the axis of rotation
Directly proportional to the square of its radial distance from the axis of rotation
questions.expl: In forced vortex motion (like a rotating solid body), tangential velocity v = ωr, directly proportional to radius.

questions.text: Bernoulli's equation assumes that
questions.expl: The derivation of Bernoulli's equation assumes a non-viscous, homogeneous fluid in steady flow, among other conditions.

questions.text: While applying the Bernoulli's equation (p/w + z + v²/2g)any section = total head, the work done on any section of the flow system, if any
options: Is added on the right side of the equation
Is added on the left side of the equation
questions.expl: Any external work done on the fluid (e.g., by a pump) is added on the same side as the total head terms of that section, i.e., the left side of this equation form.

questions.text: Euler's equation for motion of liquids is given by
options: ρ dp − g dz + v dv = 0
questions.expl: Euler's equation of motion along a streamline is written as dp/ρ + g dz + v dv = 0.

questions.text: The most familiar form of Bernoulli's equation is
options: p1/w + Z1 + v1²/2g = p2/w + Z2 + v2²/2g
questions.expl: The commonly used form states that total head (pressure, elevation and velocity heads) is constant at any section along a streamline.

questions.text: Euler's equation for the motion of liquids assumes that
options: Velocity of flow is non-uniform over the section
Flow is unsteady along the stream line
questions.expl: Euler's equation assumes the liquid is homogeneous, incompressible and frictionless.

questions.text: The main assumption of Bernoulli's equation is
options: The velocity of energy of liquid particle, across and cross-section of a pipe is uniform
No external force except gravity acts on the liquid
There is no loss of energy of the liquid while flowing
questions.expl: Bernoulli's equation assumes uniform velocity across a section, only gravity as an external force, and no energy losses — all of these together.

questions.text: If the forces are due to inertia and gravity, and the frictional resistance plays only a minor role, the design of the channels is made by comparing
questions.expl: When inertia and gravity forces dominate (as in open channel design), the Froude number is the governing similarity parameter.

questions.text: The differential equation dp/ρ + g dz + v dv = 0 for fluid motion is suggested by
questions.expl: This is Euler's differential equation of motion for an ideal fluid along a streamline.

questions.expl: Bernoulli's equation strictly holds when the energy correction factor is unity, the flow is incompressible, and it is ideal (frictionless) and irrotational.

questions.expl: This standard form of Bernoulli's equation requires an ideal fluid, steady, laminar flow, along a streamline — conditions 1, 2, 3 and 5.

questions.text: The co-efficient of discharge (Cd)
options: For an orifice is more than that for a mouthpiece
For internal mouthpiece is more than external mouthpiece
For a mouthpiece is more than that for an orifice
questions.expl: A mouthpiece, by guiding the jet and reducing contraction losses, typically has a higher coefficient of discharge than a plain orifice.

questions.text: Bernoulli's equation assumes that
options: Flow is along the stream line
questions.expl: Per the given key, the key underlying assumption highlighted here is that the flow is steady.

questions.text: The most common device for measuring discharge through channels is
questions.expl: A venturi flume is the most common device used specifically for measuring discharge in open channels.

questions.text: Navier-Stroke equation
options: only force of compressibility is neglected
both force of compressibility and force of turbulence are neglected
forces of compressibility, turbulence and velocity are neglected
questions.expl: The Navier-Stokes equations are the most general equations of fluid motion, in which no force (pressure, gravity, or viscous) is neglected.

questions.text: The term z in the total energy expression p/ρg + v²/2g + z represents
questions.expl: In the total energy expression, the elevation term z is interpreted here as representing potential (positional) energy per unit weight.

questions.text: Bernoulli equation finds its application in
questions.expl: Bernoulli's equation underlies the working principle of the pitot tube, venturimeter, and orifice meter alike.

questions.text: Which one of the following is not used for measuring flow in a pipe
questions.expl: A venturi flume is used for open-channel flow measurement, not for measuring flow within a closed pipe.

questions.text: Pitot-tube is used for measurement of
questions.expl: A pitot tube measures the stagnation pressure to determine the local flow velocity at a point.

questions.text: Orifices are used to measure
questions.expl: An orifice is primarily used to measure the rate of flow (discharge) through a tank or pipe.

questions.text: Mouthpieces are used to measure
questions.expl: Like orifices, mouthpieces are used to determine the rate of flow (discharge) of a liquid.

questions.text: The ratio of the actual velocity of a jet of water at vena-contracta to the theoretical velocity is known as
questions.expl: The coefficient of velocity Cv is defined as the ratio of actual to theoretical jet velocity at the vena contracta.

questions.text: The ratio of actual discharge of a jet of water to its theoretical discharge is known as
questions.expl: The coefficient of discharge Cd is the ratio of the actual discharge to the theoretical discharge.

questions.text: The ratio of the area of the jet of water at vena-contracta to the area of orifice is known as
questions.expl: The coefficient of contraction Cc is the ratio of the jet's cross-sectional area at vena contracta to the orifice area.

questions.text: Pitot-tube is used to measure
questions.expl: A pitot tube measures the local (point) velocity of flow via the stagnation pressure it senses.

questions.text: Venturimeter is used to measure
questions.expl: A venturimeter is designed specifically to measure the rate of discharge through a pipe.

questions.text: Total head of a liquid particle in motion is the sum of
options: Potential head, kinetic head and pressure head
questions.expl: Total head in Bernoulli's equation is the sum of elevation (potential), velocity (kinetic), and pressure heads.

questions.text: Energy equation is usually applicable to
questions.expl: Bernoulli's/energy equation in its standard form is applicable to steady flow along a streamline.

questions.text: A venturimeter is preferable to an orifice meter because
questions.expl: The gradually tapering venturimeter causes significantly less energy loss compared to the sudden contraction of an orifice meter.

questions.text: A large Reynold number is an indication of
questions.expl: A large Reynolds number indicates that inertial forces dominate over viscous forces, characteristic of highly turbulent flow.

questions.text: Pitot tube is used to measure the velocity head of
questions.expl: A pitot tube senses the stagnation pressure to determine the velocity head of a flowing fluid.

questions.text: For measuring flow by a venturimeter, it should be installed in
options: In any direction and in any location
questions.expl: A venturimeter, being based on Bernoulli's equation which accounts for elevation, can be installed in any orientation.

questions.text: A piezometer cannot be used for pressure measurement in pipe when
options: Fluid in the pipe is a gas
questions.expl: A piezometer requires a visible liquid column, so it cannot be used to measure pressure when the pipe fluid is a gas.

questions.text: The coefficient of discharge (cd) of an orifice varies with
questions.expl: The coefficient of discharge of an orifice depends on the Reynolds number of the flow through it.

questions.text: The losses are maximum in
questions.expl: Turbulent flow generally produces the greatest energy losses due to intense mixing and higher wall shear stress.

questions.text: In a venturimeter, length of divergent cone as compared to the length of convergent cone is
questions.expl: The divergent (recovery) cone of a venturimeter is made longer than the convergent cone to minimize flow separation and energy loss.

questions.text: Hydraulic grade line for any flow system as compared to energy line is
questions.expl: Since the hydraulic grade line excludes the velocity head, it always lies below the total energy line.

questions.text: Size of a venturimeter is specified by
questions.expl: A venturimeter's size is conventionally specified in terms of its throat diameter.

questions.text: Bernoulli's equation cannot be applied when the flow is
questions.expl: The simple form of Bernoulli's equation is invalid for rotational, turbulent, or unsteady flow, since it assumes ideal, steady, irrotational conditions.

questions.text: Indicate the incorrect statement: for Bernoulli's equation
options: The fluid must be an ideal gas
questions.expl: Bernoulli's equation requires an ideal (frictionless) fluid, not specifically an ideal gas, making that statement incorrect.

questions.text: A pitot tube is used to measure
questions.expl: A pitot tube measures the local velocity of flow by sensing the stagnation pressure.

questions.text: If Cv, Cc, Cd and Cr are the hydraulic coefficients of an orifice, then
questions.expl: The coefficient of discharge is the product of the coefficient of contraction and the coefficient of velocity: Cd = Cc·Cv.

questions.text: In an inclined position, a Venturimeter
questions.expl: Because Bernoulli's equation accounts for elevation change, a correctly applied venturimeter gives the same discharge reading regardless of orientation.

questions.text: An orifice is called a large orifice if water head is
options: twice the diameter of the orifice
thrice the diameter of the orifice
four times the diameter of the orifice
five times the diameter of the orifice
questions.expl: An orifice is classified as 'large' when the head of water above it is less than about five times the orifice diameter.

questions.text: Discharge through a totally submerged orifice, is directly proportional to
options: difference in elevation of water surfaces
square root of the difference in elevation of water surface
reciprocal of the area of the opening
questions.expl: For a submerged orifice, discharge Q = Cd·A√(2gΔh), so Q is proportional to the square root of the head difference.

questions.text: With a clinging nappe of a weir, the excess discharge is
questions.expl: A clinging nappe (where the sheet of water sticks to the weir face rather than springing clear) is associated with an excess discharge of about 25–30%.

questions.text: In flowing liquids pitot tubes are used to measure
questions.expl: A pitot tube is used to measure the local velocity of a flowing liquid via its stagnation pressure.

questions.text: How hot wire anemometer is used to measure
questions.expl: A hot-wire anemometer measures gas velocity by sensing the cooling effect of the flow on a heated wire.

questions.text: The theoretical value of coefficient of contraction of a sharp edged orifice is
questions.expl: The theoretical (and commonly used) value of coefficient of contraction for a sharp-edged orifice is about 0.611.

questions.text: Which of the following is used to measure the discharge?
questions.expl: A venturimeter is specifically designed to measure the discharge (flow rate) through a pipe.

questions.text: The pitot static tube measures
options: Difference in total and dynamic pressure
questions.expl: A pitot-static tube directly measures the dynamic pressure by taking the difference between stagnation and static pressures.

questions.text: Select the incorrect statement
options: The pressure intensity at vena-contracta is atmospheric
Streamlines are parallel throughout the jet at vena-contracta
Coefficient of contraction is always less than one
questions.expl: At the vena contracta the jet cross-section is actually at its minimum, i.e., contraction is maximum (not least) there, making this statement incorrect.

questions.text: Coefficient of velocity of venturimeter
options: Is equal to the coefficient of discharge of venturimeter
questions.expl: Since a venturimeter has negligible contraction, its coefficient of velocity is essentially equal to its coefficient of discharge.

questions.text: Which of the following has highest coefficient of discharge?
questions.expl: A venturimeter, with its smoothly tapering passage and minimal losses, has the highest coefficient of discharge among these devices.

questions.text: A streamline is a line
options: Connecting mid points of a flow cross-section
Connecting points of equal velocity in a flow field
Tangent to which at any point gives the direction of velocity vector at that point
The line of flow, normal to which at any point gives the velocity vector
questions.expl: A streamline is defined such that the tangent at any point along it gives the direction of the velocity vector at that point.

questions.text: A pathline represents
options: Mean direction of a number of particles at the same instant of time
Trace made by a single particle over a period of time
Instantaneous picture of positions of all particles in the flow which passed a given point
Drawn normal to the velocity vector at any point
questions.expl: A pathline is the actual trajectory traced by a single fluid particle over a period of time.

questions.text: The path traced by a single particle of smoke issuing from a cigarette is
questions.expl: The trace followed by one particle (of smoke) over time is, by definition, a pathline.

questions.text: There is no geometrical distinction between the streamline, path line and streak line in case of
questions.expl: In steady flow, the flow pattern does not change with time, so streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines all coincide.

questions.text: Mark the wrong statement
options: Streamlines cannot start or end anywhere except at the interface or infinity
Streamline spacing varies directly as the flow velocity
Streamlines can meet at a stagnation point where the velocity is zero
The flow is only along the streamline and not across it
questions.expl: Streamline spacing actually varies inversely with flow velocity (closer spacing indicates higher velocity), so this statement is wrong.

questions.text: For a two-dimensional flow field, the equation of a streamline is given as
questions.expl: The streamline equation in 2D flow is dx/u = dy/v, ensuring the velocity vector is tangent to the streamline everywhere.

questions.text: One dimensional flow means
options: Flow which neglects changes in transverse direction
questions.expl: One-dimensional flow treats flow properties as varying only along the flow direction, neglecting variations across the cross-section.

questions.text: Steady flow occurs when
options: Conditions do not change with time at any point
Conditions are the same at adjacent points at any instant
Only the velocity vector at any point does not change with time, i.e., ∂V/∂t is constant
questions.expl: Steady flow is defined by flow properties (velocity, pressure, etc.) remaining constant with time at any fixed point.

questions.text: Uniform flow occurs when
options: There is constant discharge through a pipeline
Conditions at any point in the flow field practically remain constant as time elapses
The velocity vector at any point remains constant
At any given instant, the velocity vector at every point in the flow field is identical in magnitude and direction
questions.expl: Uniform flow means that at a given instant, velocity is the same in magnitude and direction at every point in the flow field.

questions.text: In Uniform flow, the velocities of fluid particles are
options: The fluid particles move in well-defined paths
questions.expl: In uniform flow, the velocity is the same at all sections/points along the flow at a given instant.

questions.text: The flow of liquid through a tapering pipe at constant rate is
questions.expl: Constant rate makes the flow steady, but the tapering pipe (changing cross-section) makes velocity vary with position, i.e., non-uniform.

questions.text: Which of the following represents steady uniform flow?
options: Flow through a diverging duct at constant rate
Flow through a diverging duct at any increasing rate
Flow through a long pipe at constant rate
Flow through a long pipe at decreasing rate
questions.expl: Constant discharge through a long pipe of uniform section gives both steady (no time variation) and uniform (no spatial variation) flow.

questions.text: Which of the following represents steady non-uniform flow?
options: Constant discharge through a long straight pipe
Steadily decreasing flow through a reducing section
Steadily increasing flow through a long straight pipe of same section
Flow through an expanding tube at constant rate
questions.expl: Constant-rate flow through an expanding tube is steady in time but non-uniform in space due to the changing cross-section.

questions.text: Which of the following represents unsteady-uniform flow?
options: Steadily decreasing flow through a reducing section
Flow through an expanding tube at any increasing rate
Flow through a long pipe at decreasing rate
Flow through a long pipe at constant rate
questions.expl: A long uniform pipe keeps the flow spatially uniform, but a decreasing rate makes it unsteady in time.

questions.text: Which of the following represents unsteady non-uniform flow?
options: Discharge through a river at a bridge site during flood
Flow through an expanding tube at any increasing rate
Flow through a reducing section at constant rate
Flow through a long pipe at decreasing rate
questions.expl: River flow at a bridge during a flood varies both with time (unsteady) and along the channel geometry (non-uniform).

questions.text: Identify the statements pertaining to laminar flow
options: Fluid particles exhibit an irregular pattern of flow
Fluid flows through a narrow passage
Momentum transfer is on macroscopic level
The injection of smoke or dye shows considerable lateral dispersion
questions.expl: Per the given key, laminar flow is characterized here as occurring through a narrow passage (consistent with low Reynolds number conditions).

questions.text: For a streamline flow, velocity at a certain point is
questions.expl: In steady streamline flow, the velocity at a fixed point remains constant and does not change with time.

questions.text: Indicate the turbulent flow conditions amongst the following
options: Rise of water in plants through roots
Flow of oil in measuring instruments
Movement of blood in the arteries of a human body
questions.expl: Per the given key, blood flow in arteries is identified as exhibiting turbulent flow characteristics among these options.

questions.text: If φ is the potential function in two-dimensional flow field, then the velocity components u and v are defined as
questions.expl: The velocity potential defines velocity components as u = ∂φ/∂x and v = −∂φ/∂y (sign convention as given).

questions.text: A velocity potential function exists only for
questions.expl: A velocity potential function can be defined only for irrotational flow, since it requires the flow to satisfy zero vorticity.

questions.text: Which is not true in the context of velocity potential function?
options: Is defined as the integral of the tangential velocity component along a closed contour
Exists for irrotational motion of fluids whether compressible or incompressible
Lines of constant velocity potential function are normal to the streamlines
questions.expl: This description (integral of tangential velocity around a closed contour) actually defines circulation, not the velocity potential function, making it the false statement.

questions.text: The existence of velocity potential in a flow field is indicative of the fact that
options: Circulation around any closed contour must have a finite value
Flow satisfies the conditions of irrotational motion
Flow is continuous irrespective of it being rotational or irrotational
questions.expl: A velocity potential exists only when the flow is irrotational, so its existence directly indicates irrotational motion.

questions.text: Select the correct statement about equipotential line
options: Connects the mid points of a flow cross-section
Has no velocity component tangential to it
Lies orthogonal to streamlines for the flow pattern
questions.expl: Equipotential lines are always orthogonal to streamlines in a flow net, since velocity is normal to lines of constant φ.

questions.text: For irrotational flow
questions.expl: For irrotational flow, the potential function φ and stream function ψ satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann-type relation ∂φ/∂x = ∂ψ/∂y.

questions.text: The relation ∂²φ/∂x² + ∂²φ/∂y² = 0 for an irrotational flow is referred to as
questions.expl: This second-order PDE, satisfied by the velocity potential for irrotational flow, is the Laplace equation.

questions.text: Which of the following statements are true for two-dimensional flow field?
options: If φ exists, ψ will also exist
If ψ exists, φ will also exist
If φ exists, the flow will be rotational
If ψ exists, flow will be either rotational or irrotational
questions.expl: A stream function ψ can be defined for any 2D flow satisfying continuity, whether the flow is rotational or irrotational; φ exists only for the irrotational case.

questions.text: A control volume refers to
questions.expl: A control volume is a fixed region in space through which fluid may flow, used for applying conservation laws.

questions.text: The property of stream function ψ is
options: ψ is constant everywhere on any streamline
The flow around any path in the fluid is zero for continuous flow
The rate of change of ψ with distance in an arbitrary direction is proportional normal to that direction
questions.expl: All these are standard properties of the stream function: it is constant along a streamline, and its directional derivatives relate to velocity components normal to that direction.

questions.text: The continuity equation
options: Expresses the relationship between work and energy
Relates the momentum per unit volume between two points on a stream line
Relates mass rate of flow along a stream line
Requires that Newton's second law of motion be satisfied at every point in fluid
questions.expl: The continuity equation is a statement of mass conservation, relating the mass flow rate at different points along the flow.

questions.text: If u, v, w are the components of the velocity of a moving particle, the equation dx/u = dy/v = dz/w represents
questions.expl: This streamline equation involving all three velocity components (u, v, w) and coordinates represents three-dimensional flow.

questions.text: A steady uniform flow is through
options: a long pipe at decreasing rate
a long pipe at constant rate
an expanding tube at constant rate
an expanding tube at increasing rate
questions.expl: Constant-rate flow through a uniform (non-expanding) long pipe is both steady and uniform.

questions.text: Uniform flow is said to occur when
options: Size and shape of the cross section in a particular length remain constant
Size and shape of the cross section change along a length
Frictional loss in the particular length of the channel will be more than the drop in its elevation
Frictional loss in the particular length of the channel will be less than the drop in elevation
questions.expl: Uniform flow requires the size and shape of the flow cross-section to remain constant along the length considered.

questions.text: A fluid particle may possess the displacement of
questions.expl: In general fluid motion, a fluid particle can undergo translation, rotation, and distortion (linear and angular deformation) simultaneously.

questions.text: A non-uniform steady flow is through
options: a long tube at a decreasing rate
an expanding tube at constant rate
an expanding tube at increasing rate
a long pipe at increasing rate
questions.expl: Constant discharge through an expanding tube keeps the flow steady in time, while the changing cross-section makes it non-uniform in space.

questions.text: In steady flow, which one of the following changes with time
questions.expl: By definition of steady flow, none of the flow properties (velocity, pressure, density) change with time at a fixed point.

questions.text: The flow in which each liquid particle has a definite path and the paths of adjacent particles do not cross each other, is called
questions.expl: This description of orderly, non-crossing particle paths is the defining characteristic of streamline (laminar) flow.

questions.text: The flow in a channel is said to be non-uniform, if
options: Free water surface of an open channel is not parallel to the bed of channel
Head needed to overcome frictional resistance is less than the drop in elevation of channel bed
Head needed to overcome friction resistance is more than the drop in elevation of channel bed
questions.expl: Non-uniform channel flow is characterised by all these conditions together: a non-parallel water surface and an imbalance between friction head and bed-elevation drop.

questions.text: 'Flow net' can be drawn only if the flow is
questions.expl: A flow net (orthogonal grid of streamlines and equipotential lines) can only be constructed for irrotational flow, since it requires a velocity potential.

questions.text: For the two dimensional flow, the stream function is given by ψ = 2xy. The velocity at a point (3, 4) is
questions.expl: u = ∂ψ/∂y = 2x = 6, v = −∂ψ/∂x = −2y = −8; resultant velocity = √(6² + 8²) = 10 m/s.

questions.text: Equation of continuity of fluids is applicable only if
questions.expl: The continuity equation, in the given generalized sense, is stated to require steady, compressible-accommodating, and one-dimensional flow together as per this key.

questions.text: The imaginary line drawn such that the tangents at its all points indicate the direction of the velocity of the fluid particles at each point, is called
questions.expl: This is, by definition, a streamline: an imaginary line tangent to which gives the local velocity direction.

questions.text: The equation p/w + v²/2g + Z = Constant is based on the following assumptions regarding the flow of fluid
options: Steady, frictionless, incompressible and along a streamline
Steady, frictionless, uniform and along a streamline
Steady, incompressible, uniform and along a streamline
questions.expl: This is Bernoulli's equation, valid for steady, frictionless, incompressible flow along a streamline.

questions.text: The continuity equation ρ1V1A1 = ρ2V2A2 is based on the following assumption regarding flow of fluid, where ρ1 and ρ2 are mass densities
questions.expl: This general form of the continuity equation (allowing density to vary) requires only that the flow be steady.

questions.text: Irrotational flow means
options: The fluid does not rotate while moving
The fluid moves in straight lines
The net rotation of fluid particles about their mass centers is zero
questions.expl: Irrotational flow is defined by fluid particles having zero net rotation about their own mass centres, even though the overall flow path may curve.

questions.text: If the velocity, pressure, density etc., do not change at a point with respect to time, the flow is called
questions.expl: Flow properties remaining constant at a point over time is, by definition, steady flow.

questions.text: If the velocity, pressure, density etc., change at a point with respect to time, the flow is called
questions.expl: When flow properties at a point vary with time, the flow is classified as unsteady.

questions.text: If the velocity in fluid flow does not change with respect to length of direction of flow, it is called
questions.expl: Velocity remaining constant along the direction of flow (in space) defines uniform flow.

questions.text: If the density of a fluid is constant from point to point in a flow region, it is called
questions.expl: Constant density throughout the flow field, by definition, characterises incompressible flow.

questions.text: If the fluid particles move in straight lines and all the lines are parallel to the surface, the flow is called
questions.expl: Straight, parallel particle paths across the flow section describe uniform flow.

questions.text: If the fluid particles move in a zig-zag way, the flow is called
questions.expl: Irregular, zig-zag particle motion with fluctuating velocities is characteristic of turbulent flow.

questions.text: Study of fluid motion with the forces causing the flow is known as
questions.expl: Fluid dynamics specifically studies fluid motion together with the forces that cause it, as opposed to kinematics which ignores forces.

questions.text: Streamlines and Equipotential lines
options: Can be drawn graphically for viscous flow around any boundary
Can be determined mathematically for all boundary conditions
questions.expl: Streamlines and equipotential lines intersect at right angles wherever they meet, forming the basis of a flow net.

questions.text: The magnitude of the buoyant force can be determined by
questions.expl: Archimedes' principle directly gives the buoyant force as the weight of the fluid displaced by the body.

questions.text: Which of the following equations will be satisfied by irrotational flow of an incompressible fluid? (1) ∂u/∂x+∂u/∂y+∂u/∂z = 0 (2) ∂u/∂y+∂v/∂x = ∂u/∂z+∂w/∂x = ∂w/∂y+∂v/∂z = 0 (3) ∂²u/∂x²+∂²u/∂y²+∂²u/∂z² = 0 (4) ∂v/∂x = ∂u/∂y, ∂u/∂z = ∂w/∂x, ∂w/∂y = ∂v/∂z. questions.expl: Continuity for incompressible flow gives condition (1) (in its proper divergence form), while condition (3), the Laplace equation, is satisfied by the potential/velocity components for irrotational flow — together these are the applicable conditions.

questions.text: A fluid is a substance that
options: Cannot be subjected to shear forces
Cannot remain at rest under the action of any shear force
Always expands until it fills any container
questions.expl: A fluid is defined as a substance that cannot remain at rest (it deforms continuously) under the action of any shear force, however small.

questions.text: When subjected to shear force, a fluid
options: Deforms continuously only for large shear forces
Deforms continuously only for large shear stresses
Deforms continuously no matter how small the shear stress may be
questions.expl: This is the defining property of a fluid — continuous deformation occurs for any nonzero shear stress, however small.

questions.text: An ideal fluid
options: Obeys the Newton's law of viscosity
questions.expl: An ideal (perfect) fluid is assumed both incompressible and frictionless (zero viscosity).

questions.text: A fluid which obeys the relation µ = A(du/dy) is called the
questions.expl: Fluids where shear stress is directly proportional to the velocity gradient (constant viscosity) are Newtonian fluids.

questions.text: The general relation between shear stress τ and velocity gradient du/dy for a fluid can be written as τ = A(du/dy)^n + B. Which of the following is then a false statement?
options: For Newtonian fluids: n = 1 and B = 0
For dilatant fluids: n < 1 and B = 0
For ideal plastic or Bingham fluid: n = 1 and B = τ0
questions.expl: Dilatant fluids actually have n > 1 (shear-thickening), not n < 1, so this statement is false.

questions.text: If the relationship between the shear stress τ and the rate of shear strain du/dy is given by τ = K(du/dy)^n, the fluid with the exponent n < 1 is known as
questions.expl: n < 1 corresponds to shear-thinning behaviour, characteristic of pseudoplastic fluids.

questions.text: If shear stress τ and shear rate du/dy relationship of a material is plotted with τ on the y-axis and du/dy on the x-axis, the behaviour of an ideal fluid is exhibited by
options: A straight line passing through the origin and inclined to x-axis
A curved line passing through the origin
questions.expl: An ideal fluid has zero viscosity, so shear stress is always zero regardless of shear rate — it plots along the positive x-axis.

questions.text: These fluids exhibit a certain shear stress at zero shear strain rate followed by a straight line relationship between shear stress and shear strain rate
questions.expl: Ideal (Bingham) plastics require a yield stress before flow begins, after which stress varies linearly with strain rate.

questions.text: Paper pulp can be regarded as
questions.expl: Paper pulp suspensions exhibit shear-thinning behaviour and are classed as pseudoplastic fluids.

questions.text: Typical example of a Non-Newtonian fluid of pseudoplastic variety is
questions.expl: Blood is a classic shear-thinning (pseudoplastic) fluid due to suspended cells.

questions.text: Choose the correct statement about the viscosity of a liquid
options: Considerably influenced by molecular momentum transfer
Remains practically constant with temperature rise or fall
Fairly large as compared to viscosity for gases
questions.expl: Liquid viscosity, dominated by intermolecular cohesion, is typically much larger than the viscosity of gases at ordinary conditions.

questions.text: Newton's law of viscosity relates
options: Stress and strain in a fluid
Pressure, velocity and viscosity of a gas
Shear stress and rate of angular deformation in a fluid
Yield stress, viscosity and rate of angular deformation
questions.expl: Newton's law of viscosity states shear stress is proportional to the rate of angular (shear) deformation.

questions.text: The coefficient of viscosity is a property of
options: The body over which flow occurs
questions.expl: Viscosity is an intrinsic physical property of the fluid itself.

questions.text: The dimensions of a dynamic viscosity are
questions.expl: Dynamic viscosity has SI units Pa·s = kg/(m·s), giving dimensions ML⁻¹T⁻¹.

questions.text: Poise is the unit of
questions.expl: The poise (dyne·s/cm²) is the CGS unit of dynamic (absolute) viscosity.

questions.text: Correct units for kinematic viscosity are
questions.expl: Kinematic viscosity ν = µ/ρ has dimensions of area per time, i.e., m²/s.

questions.text: The viscosity of water with respect to air is about
questions.expl: Water's dynamic viscosity is roughly 50 times that of air at ordinary temperatures.

questions.text: SI unit of viscosity is
questions.expl: 1 Pa·s (SI unit) equals 10 poise (CGS unit).

questions.text: The multiplying factor for converting one stoke into m2/s is
questions.expl: 1 stoke = 1 cm²/s = 10⁻⁴ m²/s.
