questions.expl: ν = µ/ρ = 0.012 poise / 0.93 (specific gravity) works out to about 1.29 centistokes.

questions.text: The density of a fluid is sensitive to changes in temperature and pressure. The fluid will be known as
questions.expl: A fluid whose density changes appreciably with pressure/temperature is termed compressible.

questions.text: Choose the correct statement in the context of bulk modulus and coefficient of compressibility
options: The bulk modulus of elasticity of a fluid is the same as its coefficient of compressibility
Most of the liquids have a low value of bulk modulus
The bulk modulus is not influenced by changes in pressure and temperature
The relative change of volume per unit pressure is called the coefficient of compressibility
questions.expl: Coefficient of compressibility is defined as the fractional volume change per unit rise in pressure (reciprocal of bulk modulus).

questions.text: The bulk modulus of elasticity of a fluid is defined as
questions.expl: Bulk modulus K = −dp/(dV/V), the pressure change needed for a given fractional volume change.

questions.text: Which one of the following is an example of non-Newtonian fluid
questions.expl: Blood exhibits shear-thinning behaviour and does not obey Newton's law of viscosity linearly.

questions.text: A unit cubic metre of water is subjected to a pressure of 10 bar. Then a change in the volume of water amounts to (for water, bulk modulus k = 2×10^9 Pa)
Measure of the effect of compressibility in fluid flow is the magnitude of a dimensionless parameter known as
questions.expl: Mach number (velocity/speed of sound) quantifies compressibility effects in flow.

questions.text: The bulk modulus of water with respect to air is about
questions.expl: Water is far less compressible than air, with bulk modulus roughly 20,000 times greater.

questions.text: Select the correct statement
options: Higher is the bulk modulus, lower is the compressibility
For an adiabatic process the bulk modulus equals the pressure
The bulk modulus is independent of both pressure and temperature
The bulk modulus of a liquid is less than that of a solid
questions.expl: Bulk modulus and compressibility are inversely related by definition.

questions.text: All liquid surfaces tend to stretch. This phenomenon is called
questions.expl: Surface tension is the tendency of a liquid surface to contract/behave like a stretched membrane.

questions.text: Surface tension is a phenomenon due to
options: Adhesion between liquid and solid molecules
questions.expl: Surface tension arises from the cohesive attraction between liquid molecules at the free surface.

questions.text: The dimensions of surface tension in [F, L, T] notation system are
questions.expl: Surface tension is force per unit length, giving dimensions FL⁻¹.

questions.text: Falling drops of water become spherical due to
questions.expl: Surface tension minimizes surface area, and a sphere has the minimum surface area for a given volume.

questions.text: Soap helps in cleaning clothes because
options: There occurs a change in the chemical constituents of soap
Surface tension of the solution is decreased
questions.expl: Soap lowers the surface tension of water, allowing it to wet and penetrate fabric better to lift dirt.

questions.text: Oil spreads on the surface of water because
options: Oil is less dense than water
Oil has less surface tension than water
questions.expl: Oil having lower surface tension than water causes it to spread thinly over the water surface.

questions.text: Which of the following statement is wrong in the context of surface tension?
options: Surface tension represents the tendency of a liquid surface to contract to form minimum surface energy
It acts in the plane of the interface normal to any line in the surface
Has maximum value at the critical temperature of a liquid
The addition of organic solutes like soap or detergent considerably reduces the surface tension of water
questions.expl: Surface tension actually falls to zero at the critical temperature, not reaches a maximum there, making this statement wrong.

questions.text: Which of the following phenomenon is not attributable to the fluid characteristic property of surface tension?
options: Spherical shape of a droplet of liquid
Formation of bubbles and discontinuity in flow systems
Dust particles collecting on water surface
questions.expl: Dust particles resting on a water surface are not primarily a surface-tension-driven fluid phenomenon like the others listed.

questions.text: Capillary action is due to
options: Adhesion of liquid particles to a surface
questions.expl: Capillary rise/depression results from the combined effects of cohesion (within the liquid) and adhesion (to the tube wall).

questions.text: The weight of liquid that rises in a tube due to capillary action is supported by the
options: Friction on the walls of the tube
questions.expl: The vertical component of the surface tension force acting around the tube's circumference balances the weight of the raised liquid column.

questions.text: Capillary rise and depression
options: Depend solely upon the surface tension of the liquid
Are influenced by viscosity of the liquid
Depend upon the pressure difference between the liquid and the environment
Depend upon surface tension of the liquid as well as the material of the tube
questions.expl: Capillary rise depends on surface tension and also on the tube material (via contact angle) and diameter.

questions.text: The height of liquid in a capillary tube
options: Increases with a decrease in the diameter of tube
Increases with an increase in specific weight of the liquid
Decreases with an increase in surface tension
Is independent of the orientation of tube
questions.expl: Capillary rise h = 4σcosθ/(wd), so it increases as tube diameter decreases.

questions.text: Water rises to a height of 15 mm in a capillary tube of 10 mm radius. The corresponding rise in a capillary of 5 mm radius would be
questions.expl: Since h ∝ 1/r, halving the radius doubles the rise: 15 × (10/5) = 30 mm.

questions.text: To avoid a correction for the effect of capillary in manometers, the minimum diameter of tube should be
questions.expl: A manometer tube diameter of at least about 6 mm is generally recommended to keep capillary effects negligible.

questions.text: The rise of oil in the wick of an oil lamp may be attributed to
options: adhesion between the oil and the wick material
pressure difference between the liquid and environment
questions.expl: Oil climbs the wick's fine fibres via capillary action.

questions.text: Ball pen works on the principle of
questions.expl: Ink flow to the ball-point tip is governed largely by surface tension effects.

questions.text: At a liquid-air-solid interface, the contact angle θ measured in the liquid is less than 90°. This indicates that the liquid is
options: Does not form a stable bubble
questions.expl: A contact angle less than 90° indicates the liquid wets the solid surface.

questions.text: For a liquid droplet, the internal pressure in excess of outside pressure is given by (where σ is the surface tension and d is diameter of the droplet)
questions.expl: For a liquid droplet with a single surface, the excess internal pressure is Δp = 4σ/d.

questions.text: The pressure inside a soap bubble of 50 mm diameter is 25 N/m2 above the outside atmospheric pressure. The surface tension in soap film would be
questions.expl: For a soap bubble (two surfaces), Δp = 8σ/d ⟹ σ = Δp·d/8 = 25×0.05/8 ≈ 0.156 N/m.

questions.text: When two gas bubbles of radii r and 2r are in equilibrium with the surrounding liquid, the pressure inside the large bubble is
options: Half the pressure inside the smaller bubble
Equal to the pressure inside the smaller bubble
Twice the pressure inside the smaller bubble
Four times the pressure inside the smaller bubble
questions.expl: Since Δp ∝ 1/r, the bubble with twice the radius has half the excess pressure of the smaller one.

questions.text: The vapour pressure is the characteristic fluid property involved in the phenomenon of
options: Water hammer in a pipe flow
Rise of sap in a tree
Spherical shape of rain water drops
questions.expl: Cavitation occurs when local pressure drops to the liquid's vapour pressure, causing vapour bubbles to form.

questions.text: In the phenomenon of cavitation, the characteristic fluid property involved is
questions.expl: Cavitation is directly tied to the fluid's vapour pressure at the local temperature.

questions.text: Identify the wrong statement
options: Viscosity of a gas increases with temperature
Surface tension of a liquid decreases with temperature
Liquid rises in a capillary tube when angle of contact is acute
Meniscus of liquid in a capillary tube is convex in shape when the adhesive force between the liquid and gas is greater than the cohesive force between the liquid molecules
questions.expl: A convex meniscus (like mercury) actually occurs when cohesion between liquid molecules exceeds adhesion to the solid, making this statement wrong.

questions.text: All of the following statements are correct, except
options: There is one-to-one correspondence between Hook's law of elasticity and Newton's law of viscosity
For an ideal fluid µ = 0, ρ = constant and k = ∞
In a capillary tube, the meniscus of water is concave upwards while the meniscus of mercury is convex upwards
For a perfect gas k = p for an isothermal compression process and k = γp for an isentropic process
questions.expl: Hooke's law (stress ∝ strain) and Newton's law of viscosity (stress ∝ strain rate) are only analogous, not a strict one-to-one correspondence, making this the exception.

questions.text: Pascal-second is the unit of
questions.expl: The SI unit of dynamic viscosity is the pascal-second (Pa·s).

questions.text: An ideal fluid is
options: One which obeys Newton's law of viscosity
questions.expl: An ideal fluid is defined as frictionless (inviscid) and incompressible.

questions.text: The unit of kinematic viscosity is
questions.expl: Kinematic viscosity has units of area/time, i.e., cm²/sec (the stoke) in CGS.

questions.text: If the dynamic viscosity of a fluid is 0.5 poise and specific gravity is 0.5, then the kinematic viscosity of that fluid in stokes is
The viscosity of a gas
options: Is independent of pressure for very high pressure intensities
questions.expl: Gas viscosity is governed by molecular momentum transfer, which increases with temperature.

questions.text: The intensity of pressure developed by surface tension of 0.075 N/m in a droplet of water of 0.075 mm diameter is
Surface tension of water
questions.expl: Surface tension rises as temperature falls, since molecular thermal agitation (which weakens cohesion) is reduced.

questions.text: One kilo-Pascal is equivalent to
If a liquid has greater cohesion than adhesion with the solid, then the liquid in the capillary tube will
questions.expl: When cohesion dominates (e.g., mercury), the liquid is depressed in the capillary and forms a convex meniscus.

questions.text: Calculate the specific weight of 1 litre of a liquid which weighs 7 N
questions.expl: Specific weight = weight/volume = 7 N / 0.001 m³ = 7000 N/m³.

questions.text: One Poise = ? N-sec/m2
questions.expl: 1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s = 10⁻¹ N·s/m².

questions.text: A real fluid is any fluid which has
questions.expl: A real (as opposed to ideal) fluid possesses viscosity, which produces friction and shear resistance.

questions.text: The dimension of the dynamic viscosity in [F, L, T] notation system is
questions.expl: In the FLT system, dynamic viscosity has dimensions F L⁻¹T.

questions.text: Density in terms of viscosity is
options: Ratio of kinematic viscosity to dynamic viscosity
Ratio of dynamic viscosity to kinematic viscosity
Product of dynamic viscosity and kinematic viscosity
questions.expl: Since ν = µ/ρ, rearranging gives ρ = µ/ν, the ratio of dynamic to kinematic viscosity.

questions.text: What is the dimension formula of bulk modulus of elasticity?
questions.expl: Bulk modulus has the dimensions of pressure, ML⁻¹T⁻².

questions.text: The ratio of density of oil to the density of water is 0.75. It corresponds to
questions.expl: The ratio of a substance's density to that of water (reference fluid) is its specific gravity.

questions.text: Inside pressure in a hollow soap bubble in the air is (where d is the diameter of the bubble)
questions.expl: A soap bubble has two liquid surfaces, doubling the single-surface result to give Δp = 8σ/d.

questions.text: When two layers of a fluid separated by dy move over the other with a difference of velocity dv, causing a shearing stress τ = µ(du/dy), where µ is known as
questions.expl: µ in Newton's law of viscosity is variously termed coefficient of viscosity, absolute viscosity, or dynamic viscosity — all equivalent.

questions.text: An ideal flow of a liquid obeys
questions.expl: Mass conservation (continuity equation) is a basic requirement satisfied by ideal flow.

questions.text: Liquids
options: are not affected by change in pressure and temperature
questions.expl: Liquids take the shape of their container while retaining a fixed volume, i.e., they have no definite shape of their own.

questions.text: If cohesion between the molecules of a fluid is more than adhesion between the fluid and glass, the free level of fluid in a dipped glass tube will be
options: higher than the surface of liquid
same as the surface of liquid
lower than the surface of liquid
questions.expl: Stronger cohesion than adhesion (e.g., mercury in glass) causes the liquid level in the tube to be depressed.

questions.text: Cavitation is caused by
questions.expl: Cavitation occurs when local pressure drops to the vapour pressure — fundamentally a low-pressure phenomenon.

questions.text: Due to decrease of diameter of the droplet, inside pressure intensity
questions.expl: Since Δp = 4σ/d, a smaller diameter increases the internal excess pressure.

questions.text: Fluids change the volume under external pressure due to
questions.expl: Compressibility describes a fluid's volume change in response to applied pressure.

questions.text: Molecules of fluids get attracted due to
questions.expl: Cohesion is the mutual attractive force between molecules of the same fluid.

questions.text: The equation τ = µ(dv/dy) for the viscosity is suggested by
questions.expl: This is Newton's law of viscosity.

questions.text: Specific weight of liquid
options: Does not remain constant at every place
Varies from place to place on the earth
Does not vary on any other planet
questions.expl: Specific weight (ρg) depends on local gravitational acceleration, which varies slightly across the earth's surface.

questions.text: In C.G.S. system the unit of viscosity is
questions.expl: The CGS unit of dynamic viscosity is the poise.

questions.text: Mass density of liquid (ρ) is given by
questions.expl: Mass density is mass per unit volume; the other forms are dimensionally equivalent expressions used in different unit systems.

questions.text: A body of dimensions 1.5 m × 1.0 m × 2 m weighs 3000 kg in water. Its specific gravity is
questions.expl: Volume = 1.5×1×2 = 3 m³; density = 3000/3 = 1000 kg/m³, giving specific gravity ≈ 1.0.

questions.text: A rise or fall of liquid in a glass tube of a very small diameter when dipped is
options: Inversely proportional to the force per unit length of periphery
Directly proportional to the sine of the angle of contact
Directly proportional to the specific weight of liquid
Inversely proportional to the diameter of the glass tube
questions.expl: From h = 4σcosθ/(wd), capillary rise/fall is inversely proportional to tube diameter.

questions.text: Practical fluids possess
questions.expl: Real (practical) fluids exhibit viscosity, surface tension, and compressibility, unlike idealized fluids.

questions.text: Capillary rise of water is
options: inversely proportional to diameter of the tube
questions.expl: From h = 4σcosθ/(wd), rise increases with surface tension and decreases with density and tube diameter — all listed relations hold.

questions.text: For a fluid at rest
options: The shear stress depends upon the coefficient of viscosity
The shear stress is zero only on horizontal planes
The shear stress is maximum on a plane inclined at 45-degree to the horizontal
questions.expl: In a static fluid there is no relative motion between layers, so shear stress is zero everywhere.

questions.text: All fluids exert
options: Pressure in the direction of flow only
Pressure in the direction of force of gravity
Equal pressure in x, y and z-plane
questions.expl: By Pascal's law, pressure at a point in a static fluid acts equally in all directions.

questions.text: For warships, metacentric height of a ship should vary between
questions.expl: Warships require a moderate metacentric height (about 1–2 m) balancing stability with comfortable roll.

questions.text: The time period of oscillation of a floating body
options: Is a function of buoyant force
Is independent of radius of gyration of the body about its centre of gravity
Decreases with increase in metacentric height
Is not affected by acceleration due to gravity
questions.expl: T = 2π√(k²/(g·GM)); a larger metacentric height (GM) shortens the oscillation period.

questions.text: The position of Centre of pressure on a plane surface immersed vertically in a static mass of fluid is
options: At the centroid of the submerged area
Always above the centroid of the area
Always below the centroid of the area
questions.expl: Because pressure increases with depth, the centre of pressure lies below the centroid of the submerged area.

questions.text: A vertical triangular area with vertex downward and altitude h has its base lying on the free surface of a liquid. The centre of pressure below the free surface is at a distance of
questions.expl: For this triangular geometry (vertex down, base at surface), the standard hydrostatics result gives the centre of pressure at h/2 below the surface.

questions.text: The total pressure on a plane surface inclined at an angle θ with the horizontal is equal to (where p is pressure intensity at centroid of area and A is area of plane surface)
questions.expl: Total hydrostatic force = pressure at the centroid × area, regardless of the surface's inclination.

questions.text: A vertical rectangular plane surface is submerged in water such that its top and bottom surfaces are 1.5 m and 6.0 m respectively below the free surface. The position of centre of pressure below the free surface will be a distance of
questions.expl: Using the standard formula for centre of pressure of a submerged rectangle between these depths gives approximately 4.2 m.

questions.text: The horizontal component of force on a curved surface is equal to the
options: Product of pressure intensity at its centroid and area
Force on a vertical projection of the curved surface
Weight of liquid vertically above the curved surface
Force on the horizontal projection of the curved surface
questions.expl: The horizontal component of hydrostatic force on a curved surface equals the force on its vertical projection.

questions.text: On an inclined plane, centre of pressure is located
questions.expl: Because pressure increases with depth, the centre of pressure on an inclined submerged plane lies below the centroid.

questions.text: The hydrostatic force acts through
questions.expl: By definition, the resultant hydrostatic force on a submerged surface acts through the centre of pressure.

questions.text: If H is depth of rectangle and B is width then centre of pressure below the free surface of water is
questions.expl: For a rectangular plane with its top edge at the free surface, the centre of pressure lies at 2H/3 depth.

questions.text: The centre of pressure of vertical plane immersed in a liquid is at
questions.expl: The centre of pressure generally does not coincide with the centroid, the top edge, or the bottom edge — its exact location depends on the shape and depth of submersion.

questions.text: The pressure intensity at a point in a fluid is the same in all directions only when
options: The fluid is frictionless and incompressible
The fluid has zero viscosity and is at rest
There is no motion of one fluid layer relative to an adjacent layer
questions.expl: Pascal's law (equal pressure in all directions) holds for a fluid that has zero viscosity effects and is at rest.

questions.text: One atmospheric pressure equals
questions.expl: All three values are equivalent standard expressions of one atmosphere of pressure.

questions.text: An open tank contains 1 m deep water with 50 cm depth of oil of specific gravity 0.8 above it. The intensity of pressure at the bottom of tank will be (g = 10 m/sec2)
Gauge pressure is
questions.expl: By definition, gauge pressure = absolute pressure minus atmospheric pressure.

questions.text: Atmospheric pressure varies with
questions.expl: Atmospheric pressure changes with altitude, temperature, and weather systems.

questions.text: Atmospheric pressure is equal to a water column head of
questions.expl: Standard atmospheric pressure corresponds to about 10.3 m of water column.

questions.text: The pressure less than atmospheric pressure is known as
questions.expl: Pressure below atmospheric is called suction, vacuum, or negative gauge pressure — all synonymous terms.

questions.text: Pick out the incorrect statement(s). An inverted differential manometer is most suitable if (1) the pressure difference is small (2) the pressure difference is large (3) the fluid in the pipe is a gas. On the above statements
questions.expl: Inverted manometers are best suited for small pressure differences (with liquids in pipes), so statement (2) alone — claiming large differences — is incorrect.

questions.text: Gauge pressure is
questions.expl: Per the given key, gauge pressure here is referenced against the local atmospheric pressure as the datum.

questions.text: Piezometers are used to measure
options: Pressure in water channels, pipes etc.
Difference in pressure at two points
questions.expl: A piezometer is a simple open tube used to measure static (gauge) pressure in pipes/channels.

questions.text: Manometers are used to measure
options: Pressure in water channels, pipes etc.
Difference in pressure at two points
questions.expl: Manometers typically measure the pressure difference between two points using a column of liquid.

questions.text: Differential manometers are used to measure
options: Pressure in water channels, pipes etc.
Difference in pressure at two points
questions.expl: A differential manometer specifically measures the pressure difference between two points in a system.

questions.text: One kilo Pascal is equivalent to
U-tube manometer measures
options: Difference in pressure between two points
Difference in total energy between two points
questions.expl: A U-tube manometer is commonly used to determine the pressure difference between two points.

questions.text: Bourdon gauge measures
questions.expl: A Bourdon gauge reads gauge pressure, i.e., pressure relative to the surrounding atmosphere.

questions.text: The avg. value of atmospheric pressure at sea level is
questions.expl: Standard atmospheric pressure at sea level equals 760 mm of mercury.

questions.text: Bourden's pressure gauge measures the
questions.expl: Bourdon gauges are commonly used to measure gas pressure via deformation of a curved tube.

questions.text: A piezometer cannot be used for pressure measurement in pipes when
options: The fluid in pipes is a gas
questions.expl: Piezometers rely on a visible liquid column, so they cannot be used when the pipe fluid is a gas.

questions.text: The continuity equation
options: Expresses the relation between energy and work
Requires Newton's law to be satisfied at every point
questions.expl: The continuity equation is a statement of conservation of mass, relating the mass flow rate at different sections.

questions.text: 1 pascal pressure is equal to
questions.expl: 1 Pa corresponds to roughly 0.0001 m (0.1 mm) of water column.

questions.text: Mercury is suitable for manometer because of it
options: It can easily be seen in tube
Does not stick to tube walls
It is generally not used in manometers
questions.expl: Mercury's high density allows measurement of large pressures with a comparatively short column.

questions.text: In a reaction turbine
options: Flow can be regulated without loss
There is only partial conversion of available head to velocity head before entry to runner
The outlet must be above the tail race
Water may be allowed to enter a part or whole of wheel circumference
questions.expl: In a reaction turbine, only part of the available head is converted to velocity head before the runner; the rest is converted as pressure energy within the runner itself.

questions.text: Indicate the wrong statement with respect to reaction water turbine
options: The water leaves the turbine at atmospheric pressure
The guide vanes direct the flow at proper angle
The spiral casing serves to uniformly distribute water into guide blades
The draft tube allows setting of turbine above tail race with minimum reduction in available energy
questions.expl: In a reaction turbine water leaves the runner below atmospheric pressure (recovered by the draft tube), so this statement is wrong.

questions.text: The installation of a draft tube in a reaction turbine helps to
options: transport water to downstream without eddies
convert the kinetic energy to pressure head
questions.expl: A draft tube's diverging shape reduces exit velocity, converting residual kinetic energy back into useful pressure head.

questions.text: Compared to cylindrical draft tube, a tapered draft tube
options: converts more of kinetic head into pressure head
prevents cavitation even under reduced discharges
questions.expl: A tapered (diverging) draft tube decelerates the flow more effectively, recovering more of the kinetic head as pressure head than a cylindrical one.

questions.text: In a Francis turbine, maximum efficiency is obtained when
options: relative velocity is radial at the outlet
absolute velocity is radial at the outlet, velocity of flow is constant
blade tip is radial at the outlet
questions.expl: Maximum efficiency in a Francis turbine occurs when the absolute velocity at outlet is radial (no whirl component) and the flow velocity remains constant.

questions.text: In practice, the flow ratio of a Francis turbine is found to lie in the range
questions.expl: The typical flow ratio for a Francis turbine (velocity of flow at inlet to √(2gH)) lies between about 0.15 and 0.3.

questions.text: The modern Francis turbine is essentially
questions.expl: The modern Francis turbine is a mixed-flow machine, with water entering radially and leaving axially through the runner.

questions.text: A Kaplan turbine is a
questions.expl: A Kaplan turbine is designed as an axial-flow reaction turbine suited to low heads and large discharges.

questions.text: A Kaplan turbine is suitable for
questions.expl: Kaplan turbines are used where the head available is low but the discharge is large.

questions.text: An adjustable blade propeller turbine is called
questions.expl: A propeller turbine with adjustable runner blades is specifically termed a Kaplan turbine.

questions.text: The runner vanes of a reaction turbine are made adjustable, as a Kaplan turbine, to
options: reduce the wear and tear of the runner
allow running at different speeds of rotation
operate the machine at optimum efficiency at part load conditions
permit the machine to operate under varying conditions of pressure and discharge
questions.expl: Adjustable runner blades let a Kaplan turbine maintain a favourable blade angle and hence near-optimum efficiency across a range of part-load conditions.

questions.text: Which amongst the following is false with respect to Kaplan turbine
options: it has blades of small camber to prevent separation
it employs larger guide vane angles than those in Francis turbine
it can adjust both guide vane and blade angles according to rate of discharge
it is designed for flow velocity of the mixed flow type
questions.expl: A Kaplan turbine is an axial-flow (not mixed-flow) machine, so describing its flow velocity as mixed-flow type is false.

questions.text: The value of speed ratio for a Kaplan turbine is about
questions.expl: The speed ratio for a Kaplan turbine is typically around 1.5, higher than for Francis or Pelton turbines.

questions.text: Usually the ratio of hub-diameter to the outside diameter of the runner of a Kaplan turbine is between
questions.expl: The hub-to-runner diameter ratio in a Kaplan turbine typically falls between about 0.4 and 0.6.

questions.text: Run away speed of a hydraulic turbine is the speed
options: at which there would be no damage to the turbine runner
at which the turbine runner can be allowed to run freely without load and with wicket gates wide open
questions.expl: Runaway speed is the speed the turbine would reach if the load were suddenly removed with the gates fully open.

questions.text: Critical speed of a turbine is
options: speed that will cause mechanical failure of the shaft
speed at which natural frequency of vibrations equals the number of revolutions in the same time
speed equal to synchronous speed of the generator
questions.expl: Critical speed is the rotational speed at which the shaft's natural vibration frequency coincides with the running speed, causing resonance.

questions.text: Specific speed of a turbo machine
options: is the speed of a machine having unit dimensions
related the shape rather than size of the machine
remains the same under different conditions of operation
depends only upon the head under which the machine operates
questions.expl: Specific speed is a shape parameter that characterises the runner geometry (type) rather than its physical size.

questions.text: The specific speed of a water turbine is expressed as
questions.expl: The conventional specific speed of a turbine is defined as Ns = N√P / H^(5/4).

questions.text: Specific speed of an impulse turbine (Pelton wheel) ranges from
questions.expl: Pelton wheels, used for high heads, have low specific speeds, typically in the range 10–20 (or up to about 35 for multi-jet units).

questions.text: Francis turbines are available in the following range of specific speeds
questions.expl: Francis turbines, suited to medium heads, have specific speeds typically ranging from about 50 to 250.

questions.text: High specific speed (250 – 850) and low heads (below 30 m) indicate that the turbine is
questions.expl: High specific speed combined with low head is characteristic of Kaplan (axial flow) turbines.

questions.text: Suggest the turbine that works under a head of 30 m, runs at 400 rpm and develops 15 MW power
questions.expl: Computing the specific speed for these conditions gives a high value consistent with a Kaplan turbine's operating range.

questions.text: Francis, Kaplan and propeller turbines fall under the category of
questions.expl: Francis, Kaplan, and propeller turbines all operate on the reaction principle, using both pressure and velocity changes across the runner.

questions.text: The degree of reaction of a Kaplan turbine is
options: greater than zero but less than 1/2
questions.expl: A Kaplan turbine has a degree of reaction greater than 1/2 but less than 1, reflecting substantial pressure-energy conversion in the runner.

questions.text: Mark the false statement
options: for a Pelton wheel, degree of reaction R = 0
the specific speed decreases if the degree of reaction in a turbine is increased
questions.expl: In practice, specific speed tends to increase (not decrease) as the degree of reaction increases, making this statement false.

questions.text: All of the following statements are correct, except
options: a slow runner turbine has a degree of reaction greater than 50 percent
for a 100 percent reaction turbine, the energy transfer becomes zero
in decreasing order of specific speed, the water turbines can be put as propeller turbine, Francis turbine and Pelton wheel
a bulb or tubular turbine belongs to the category of Kaplan turbine
questions.expl: A slow-runner (low specific speed) turbine such as Pelton has a low degree of reaction, not greater than 50 percent, making this statement the exception.

questions.text: The energy conversion process in the outward radial flow turbine is
options: may be by impulse or reaction
partly by impulse and partly by reaction
questions.expl: An outward radial flow turbine's energy conversion process may be designed as either purely impulse or purely reaction, depending on the type.

questions.text: Cavitation in a hydraulic turbine may occur in all likelihood
options: at the inlet to draft tube
questions.expl: Cavitation is most likely where pressure is lowest, typically at the runner outlet / draft tube inlet.

questions.text: Amongst the following, which turbine is least efficient under part load conditions?
questions.expl: A simple (fixed-blade) propeller turbine, lacking adjustable blades, suffers the most efficiency loss under part-load conditions.

questions.text: Indicate the turbine that is most efficient at part load operation
questions.expl: Per the given key, the propeller turbine is indicated as most efficient at part-load operation among these options.

questions.text: Which of the following turbine has not only a high design efficiency but that efficiency practically remains constant too over a wide range of regulation from the design condition?
questions.expl: The Kaplan turbine's adjustable blades let it maintain high, nearly constant efficiency across a wide range of loads.

questions.text: Operating characteristic curves of a turbine means the curves drawn at constant
questions.expl: Operating characteristic curves of a turbine are plotted for varying speed/power at a constant head.

questions.text: Which one of the followings is a wrong statement?
options: only the tangential component of absolute velocity is considered in the estimation of theoretical head of a turbo machine
a high head turbine has a high value of specific speed
for the same power, a turbo machine running at high specific speed will be small in size
Pelton wheel is the tangential flow turbine whereas the Propeller and Kaplan turbines are axial flow units
